analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and its companion law at the end of 2017, with no replacement.
analysis.headline: The full repeal bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in eight House committees until the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe the Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 off the books effective December 31, 2017, and restore every law those acts changed. It offers no replacement: the Medicaid expansion, subsidized marketplace coverage, protections for pre-existing conditions, and the requirement that insurers cover essential benefits would all end. The taxes that fund the law — including the surtaxes on high incomes and investment income — would be repealed with it.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households, who would stop paying the ACA's Medicare surtax and 3.8% net investment income tax; health insurers, who would be released from the guaranteed-issue and essential-benefit rules; and private student lenders, since repealing the 2010 reconciliation act would unwind the law that shifted federal student lending to the government's direct-loan program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, insurers, private student lenders

how_it_helps.text: Repeals both ACA laws effective December 31, 2017, and restores every provision of law they amended or repealed, without a replacement plan [S2][S3].

Repealing the ACA would eliminate its taxes, including the additional Medicare tax on high earners and the net investment income tax, which fall mainly on households at the top of the income distribution.

The bill also repeals the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, which included the overhaul that ended the bank-based federal student loan program in favor of direct government lending — restoring the prior law would return that business to private lenders [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who got coverage or lower costs through the ACA: those who bought subsidized marketplace plans, the states' Medicaid expansion populations, and people with pre-existing conditions who rely on the ban on denial or surcharging. The uninsured rate would rise and no replacement coverage is provided in the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: ACA marketplace and Medicaid expansion enrollees

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no replacement for the coverage it repeals: ending the ACA's Medicaid expansion, marketplace subsidies, and guaranteed-issue rules would leave millions without coverage and once again allow insurers to deny or price out people with pre-existing conditions [S2][S3].
Repeal takes effect December 31, 2017, giving states, insurers, and enrollees only months to unwind systems built around the ACA, with no transition provisions in the bill text [S3].

Supporters' good-faith case: the ACA's mandates and regulations raised premiums for people who buy their own insurance and don't qualify for subsidies, and full repeal would return them to the pre-ACA market. That market, however, was one in which insurers could decline or surcharge sick applicants, so the savings for the healthy come directly from losses in protection for the sick.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are concentrated — lower ACA taxes for top earners and fewer rules for insurers and lenders — while the costs are broad and fall on people who would lose coverage or protections. Because the bill repeals without replacing, an honest accounting is that the average enrollee who keeps paying premiums has far more to lose than to gain, and there is no offsetting program to catch those who lose coverage.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight committees on the day it was introduced; none of them held a markup, and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mo Brooks introduced the ObamaCare Repeal Act on March 24, 2017, with five Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
The Speaker referred it to eight standing committees the same day, including Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Appropriations [S5].
In the following week it was sent to subcommittees on Indian, Insular and Alaska Native Affairs (March 30) and on Health (March 31) [S5].
No committee reported the bill and no floor vote was ever scheduled; its action history ends there for the 115th Congress, which expired January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The roughly 20 million-plus people covered through ACA marketplaces and the Medicaid expansion kept their coverage and protections, since the repeal never advanced. Insurers kept a regulated market with subsidized customers, and the ACA's taxes on high incomes stayed in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: ACA enrollees, who kept their coverage

for.name: Rep. Mo Brooks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full-repeal bill on March 24, 2017.

for.name: 5 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all five were Republicans.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (and seven parallel committees)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 24, 2017 and never reported it or scheduled any action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Republican support (a sponsor and five cosponsors, all R), and in a House controlled by Republicans it still never advanced past committee referral — so no recorded vote ever separated the parties.

industries.note: Repeal frees insurers from guaranteed-issue, essential-benefit, and rate rules, but strips away the subsidies and the individual mandate that brought them millions of subsidized customers. People with pre-existing conditions would once again face denial or unaffordable pricing.

Repealing the ACA ends the additional Medicare tax on high wages and the 3.8% net investment income tax, a direct tax cut concentrated at the top. The bill's repeal is unconditional and immediate at the end of 2017.

The Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 ended the bank-based FFEL program and moved federal student lending to direct government loans; restoring pre-2010 law would hand that lending back to private banks, raising costs for borrowers.

industries.industry: Hospitals and providers serving expanded Medicaid populations
industries.note: Ending the Medicaid expansion removes coverage for millions of patients, leaving hospitals and clinics with more uncompensated care. Providers and their patients lose together under this bill.
